chunks: What are chiplets?. The question: What are chiplets?
A chiplet is a small chip designed to be one piece of a bigger system.
Instead of making one huge chip, you make several smaller dies, test them, and put the good ones into a single package that acts like one chip.
This improves yield, gets past the size limit of the printing machine, and lets each piece use the best manufacturing technology for its job.
The cost is slower, more power-hungry links between the pieces.
Compare carving a statue from one giant block of marble with building it from bricks. One crack in the marble ruins the whole block.
With bricks, you check each one and swap out a bad brick.
The joints between bricks are weaker than solid stone, though, just as links between dies are slower and use more energy than wires inside one die.
Yield falls exponentially with area.
Splitting 800 mm² into four 200 mm² chiplets moves each piece from 45% up to 82% on the same process, and a worse process (dashed) punishes big dies even harder.
Drag defect density A up to 0. 3 per cm² and the 800 mm² die falls below 10% while the 200 mm² chiplet still yields about 55%.
Monolithic die: all the functions on one piece of silicon. Chiplet: a small die made to be combined with others in one package. Yield: the fraction of dies that work.
Known good die: a die tested before assembly, so bad ones never reach the package. Die-to-die link: the short, wide connection between two chiplets.
Interposer: a thin piece of silicon with fine wiring that connects the chiplets sitting on it.
Assume 0. 1 defects per cm². An 800 mm² die has an expected 0. 8 defects, so it yields about e to the -0. 8 about 45%. A 200 mm² die yields about e to the -0. 2 about 82%.
On a 300 mm wafer you get about 29 good big dies, or about 251 good small ones.
Four small ones make one product, so the same wafer gives about 63 products instead of 29, roughly twice as many, before counting packaging cost. That is the whole idea.
"A chiplet is a small die that is one building block of a bigger chip.
You make several small dies, test them, and combine the good ones in one package so it acts like a single processor.
It wins on yield, because small dies catch fewer defects, it breaks past the reticle size limit, and it lets you mix process nodes.
The cost is slower, more power-hungry links between dies and harder packaging, test and cooling."
